title_original: At Salon Photo, Sigma Thinks Wide
excerpt_original: From October 9 to 11, Sigma sets up its Meetings space at the Salon Photo & Vidéo, in Paris. A dozen sessions bring together photographers and videographers, who share their working methods and their lens choices, from natural-light portraiture to wildlife reportage. L’article…

blocks.text: What does one come looking for at a photography fair? Cameras to weigh in the hand, lenses to screw on, test counters where you can switch from one to the other. And photographers explaining how they use them. That is Sigma’s usual wager, and it sets up a Rencontres space at the heart of the Salon, from October 8 to 11. From Friday October 9 to Sunday October 11, presentations and discussions “around the practice of the image” follow one another.

In this space, professionals, in photography and in video, detail their methods and their equipment choices, and the Japanese manufacturer takes the opportunity to show how they “select and use” its lenses. Sigma says the sessions are aimed at “all kinds of users”. The programme runs to a dozen 45-minute sessions, except for one shorter interlude devoted to aviation enthusiasts.

Friday October 9 opens at 11 a.m. with the Sigma France team, who present the new 2026 products and, according to the brand, hand over “all the keys” to plan a visit. “An ideal introduction”, it announces, with the obligatory exclamation mark. At 12:30 p.m., Nadia Vialan, creator of the blogs “Blog Photo Lumix” and “Partons en voyage” (“Let’s Travel”), runs through the Art, Contemporary and Sports lines, from ultra-wide-angle for urban exploration to telephoto for nature photography. A tour of the catalogue to work out which prime or which zoom suits which project.

At 2 p.m., the Fondation des Œuvres Sociales de l’Air (FOSA) takes the microphone for 20 minutes. A Sigma partner for ten years, it hands out, on the Rencontres space, the prizes of a contest reserved for spotters, aviation enthusiasts who watch for planes the way others watch for birds. The grand winner leaves with a Sigma lens, in keeping with a ten-year-old partnership.

blocks.caption: © Fondation des Œuvres Sociales de l’Air (FOSA)

blocks.text: Long lenses then fill the afternoon, and the 300-600mm F4 DG OS | Sports takes the lead. At 2:30 p.m., Marc Schoeffel, photographer and videographer, has been observing Alsatian wildlife for several years, birds in particular. Creator of a widely followed YouTube channel, he has built solid day-to-day experience with long focal lengths and was one of the first to test this zoom for mirrorless cameras. At 4 p.m., Olivier and Frédéric Larrey, brothers and professional photographers, take over, from Norway to Japan. On their Leica SL3 bodies, they alternate between the 200mm F2 and the 500mm F5.6, prized for their compactness when travelling, and bring out the 300-600mm for their most ambitious projects.

Saturday October 10 changes focal length and light. At 11 a.m., Lou Sonsino, a photographer based in Lille, explains her method for portraiture and family photography: intimate moments, from pregnancy to birth, documented with kindness and exclusively in natural light. Her tool, the 50mm F1.2 DG | Art, lets her do without artificial lighting, even when light is scarce. She also promises to share her way of talking with her subject to achieve a “soft and authentic” look.

At 12:30 p.m., Gardères & Dohmen take up a challenge set by Sigma. This duo, regular speakers at the space and used to professional assignments, from corporate to weddings, set aside their usual equipment to test the APS-C Contemporary range on personal and family subjects. They deliver their feedback on these compact zooms, with the idea of photographing “naturally and discreetly”.

At 2:30 p.m., Tony Noël, a Lyon-based photographer and regular collaborator of Sigma France, presents the 85mm F1.2 DG | Art, unveiled to the public for the first time at the Salon. Chosen to make the images for the international launch campaign, he describes his first shoots in the field and what this “ultra-bright” lens brings to portraiture. This is the session that doubles as a preview.

The day closes at 4 p.m. with cinema. Laurent B, Cine Specialist at Sigma France, presents the AF Cine Line range, which combines the ergonomics and design of traditional cinema lenses with the advantages of autofocus. Videographers Thibault Loosveldt and Arnaud Moro join him to recount their latest shoots with the 28-45mm T2 FF and the 28-105mm T3 FF. An odd one out at a photography fair? Let us recall that the event is called, precisely, Salon Photo & Vidéo.

We hit the road on Sunday October 11. At 11 a.m., William Chareyre, a Lyon-based photographer, recounts a trip through Southeast Asia undertaken with a precise constraint: limiting the weight and bulk of his equipment. He explains why he chose the primes and zooms of the Contemporary range to travel across Vietnam, and how this compact kit let him adapt to every reporting situation. The payoff is a practical exchange on putting together “a camera bag optimised for travel”.

At 12:30 p.m., a change of scenery with Lolita Charlet, a Lille-based portrait and fashion photographer. Her colourful world, inspired by the sixties and seventies, gives a central place to sets, styling and accessories. She presents her creative approach and her shooting with the 17-40mm F1.8 DC | Art mounted on a Fujifilm body, which allows her to produce most of her work, then her methods for building a project and her advice for directing a model with ease.

At 2:30 p.m., Marie Bouhiron looks back on her round-the-world trip, which began with a “simple objective”: to document the planet and meet the cultures that inhabit it. The word is Sigma’s, and it lands neatly in this context. She draws on a selection of her most striking images, made with a travel kit of Sigma lenses, and shares anecdotes and equipment choices.

This programme is therefore an in-house affair: each session is tied to a lens or a range, and the whole reads like a catalogue told in the first person. And the line-up has plenty to hold the attention. The camera bodies vary (Leica SL3 for the Larrey brothers, Fujifilm for Lolita Charlet), so do the genres, from wildlife reportage to fashion, and the questions are about the craft: how to direct a model, how to pack a bag, how to talk to a subject. What remains, between two talks, is to check the promises on one’s own camera, at the test counters.

The Sigma space can be visited at the Salon Photo & Vidéo, October 8 to 11, 2026, at the Grande Halle de la Villette, Paris. Full programme (in French): Salon Photo & Vidéo 2026 : le programme des Rencontres Sigma . Sigma France is offering invitations with the code SIGMA26 on the Salon ticket office .
